english.html: or set out the crimes which, for their enormity, deserve the prodigy of such a penalty, this is committed and left to the discretion of the judge <sup class="mk" data-key="ſ">ſ</sup>: who, if he sees it expedient to exercise the sword of justice upon the carcass of a man executed to death, may justly and indubitably do so <sup class="mk" data-key="t">t</sup>; singularly in France, where the judges take cognizance of crimes only extraordinarily <sup class="mk" data-key="u">u</sup>. Wherefore it ought not to be found so novel or strange that, in horror and execration of a crime, the body of a dead person should be punished <sup class="mk" data-key="x">x</sup>. As by the same reason also the law sometimes commands, in detestation of a horrible crime of brutish sodomy, that the brute beasts be punished and cruelly put to death <sup class="mk" data-key="y">y</sup>. And on this subject our canons (much milder and more gracious in penalties than the civil laws) have nevertheless willed that if a religious who has made a vow of poverty is discovered after his death to have possessed any property as his own, his body must be dug out of the sepulchre and thrown on a dunghill, or else into a privy <sup class="mk" data-key="z">z</sup>.

Today the judge who takes cognizance of a crime extraordinarily may pass what sentence he will, heavier or lighter, within reason — the text behind "the judges take cognizance of crimes only extraordinarily" (cf. annot-012).

english.html: Adjudges the goods of the said du Tilh to the
daughter procreated by his doings and of the said

Above, we have sufficiently, as it seems to me, proved <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup> that this daughter (now the sole survivor of the two children procreated by the doings of the said du Tilh and de Rols) was legitimate, by reason of the error and good faith of the said de Rols <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>; as also, in like manner, we say of the children who should be born of a priest whom the woman had married, thinking that he was a lay person and fit to marry, that for the ignorance and good faith of the woman they are legitimate <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>. Wherefore it must not be doubted that such children succeed to father and mother, and to their other kinsfolk <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>, and not only in rural and patrimonial goods, but also in fiefs and other noble goods <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>. And, to be brief, such children must in all and every respect be deemed no less legitimate than if they had been procreated, conceived and begotten of a just and legitimate

notes.gloss: Where the legitimacy of the children born to Bertrande and the impostor is argued from her good faith.

le, procreée de ſes œuures, & de ladite

lines: Ci deſſus, nous auons ſuffiſamment, ce me ſemble
prouué {a}, que ceſte fille (ores des deux enfans procreez
des œuures deſdits du Tilh, & de Rols, ſeule ſuruiuãte)
eſtoit legitime, pour raiſon de l'erreur, & bonne foy de
ladite de Rols {b}. comme auſſi en ſemblable, nous diſons
des enfans qui ſeroient nez d'vn preſtre, que la femme
auroit eſpouſé, penſant que ce fuſt vne perſonne laye, &
apte à ſe marier: que pour l'ignorance & bonne foy de
la femme, ſont legitimes {c}. Dont ne faut douter, que
tels enfans ne ſuccedent à pere, meres, & autres leurs
parens {d}, & non ſeulement és biens ruraux, & patrimo
niaux: mais encore és fiefz, & autres biens nobles {e}. &
pour faire brief, tels enfans doyuent eſtre en tout &
par tout eſtimez, non moins legitimes, que ſ'ils euſſent
eſté procree, conceus, & engendrez de iuſte, & legitime
